Let’s dive into Chapter Seven: The War on Drugs and the New Jim Crow.
As the twentieth century wound down, something deeply significant was unfolding—something that would leave its mark on millions of lives, sometimes out in the open, but often hidden in plain sight.
The so-called “war on drugs” burst onto the scene with bold promises—talk of ending crime and addiction, making neighborhoods safer, and turning things around for good.
But if you looked closer, you’d see it wasn’t really about helping everyone. In reality, it became a powerful way to keep old patterns of exclusion and control alive.
City after city, police poured into Black and brown neighborhoods. People were arrested for things as minor as holding a small amount of drugs—sometimes just for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Judges handed down harsh sentences, filling prisons with young folks who might’ve just been walking home from school, or trying to keep their heads above water.
Politicians amped up the fear, tossing around words like “superpredators” and vowing to be “tough on crime.” It made headlines and stoked resentment, but it also made these communities feel under siege.
Think about what that meant for families. Picture a teenager suddenly facing years behind bars for a single mistake. Or a mother, doing her best to keep her family together, forced to watch loved ones vanish into a maze of courts and jails.
The cycle of incarceration didn’t just punish individuals—it tore entire communities apart, making it nearly impossible to find steady work, safe housing, or even a glimmer of hope.
Most folks outside these neighborhoods? They saw only the headlines: crime statistics, mugshots, fiery political speeches. But they missed the daily reality—constant surveillance, suspicion at every turn, families left to pick up the pieces.
The language of law and order made it easy to overlook the racial disparities built into the system. Here’s something to pay attention to: the war on drugs wasn’t just about stopping crime. It was about power.
By targeting Black and brown communities, the system kept an old idea alive—that some people are just too dangerous, not to be trusted, and not deserving of compassion.
Some started calling this reality the new Jim Crow—less obvious than the old, but every bit as real. The mechanisms had changed, but the message stayed the same.
Now, in the face of all this, resistance grew in many forms. Activists rose up, demanding an end to mass incarceration and pushing for the rights of those locked out of society.
Families built networks of care, finding ways to support each other and keep hope alive, even when the struggle felt endless and lonely.
The war on drugs showed us just how quickly old ways of thinking can slip into new disguises.
So, what’s the lesson here? Changing laws is important, but it’s not enough by itself. To truly move forward, we have to change hearts and minds, and challenge the stories we tell about who belongs—and who doesn’t.
